10.3.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what are the goals of TKA?"
- "**Mechanical axis** neutral · **joint line** restored · **balanced**, equal, rectangular gaps."
- "Correct component **rotation** · good **patellofemoral tracking** → balancing is the key step."
- "Numbers → **6-3-7** = distal femoral valgus 6°, femoral external rotation 3°, slope 7°."

### The six goals
- Mechanical axis · joint line · ligament balance · equal symmetrical gaps · **rotation** · PF tracking
[[FIG: Fig 10.14 · 10.3
- One goal seen three ways → a miss in one is not rescued by the others
- TKA = **soft-tissue balancing** surgery → balancing = most important step → chapter 11
- **PF tracking** → often forgotten, especially without resurfacing

#### 6-3-7
- **6** distal femoral valgus · **3** femoral ER · **7** posterior tibial slope (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Each number varies · say "**distal femoral valgus angle**", never just "valgus angle"

### Mechanical axis
- Femoral head centre → **talar dome** centre on standing long film · **3° ± 1.5°** to vertical
[[FIG: Fig 10.15 · 10.3
- Through knee centre = neutral · medial = **varus** · lateral = valgus
- Tibial surface **87°** (≈3° varus), femur 93° → joint line parallel to the ground

#### Malalignment
- Error ≤**3°** acceptable, still aim neutral · >3° → worse outcome, lower survivorship (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Malalignment → **wear**, aseptic loosening, tibiofemoral and PF instability, patellar fracture, stiffness

### Joint line
- Landmarks → **10 mm** below lower pole of patella · 30 mm below medial epicondyle
[[FIG: Fig 10.16 · 10.3
- Also → 25 mm below lateral epicondyle · 10–15 mm above **fibular head** · Campbell: 28, 23, fibula 14
[[FIG: Fig 10.79 · 10.3
- Revision → peripheral **meniscal remnants** mark the native line (rarely found)
- **Raised** → baja · **lowered** (tibial over-cut, thin insert, short distal cut) → alta, incomplete extension, flexion instability

PITFALL — how far may the joint line move?
- Prof Sherif Khaled → up to **8 mm**, beyond = baja · Campbell → avoid elevation >**4 mm**
- Say → "**keep it within 4 mm** → more costs motion, patellar function and mid-flexion stability"

- Excess distal cut + thick insert → raised line → **pseudo-baja**, mid-flexion instability, anterior knee pain
- **CR** tolerates little joint-line change · **PS** accepts mild elevation (Campbell)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **6-3-7 · axis within 3° · line within 4 mm · up = baja**

10.4.t: Strategy: Measured Resection, Gap Balancing & Alignment
10.4.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "measured resection or gap balancing?"
- "**Measured** → cuts = implant thickness, rotation from bony landmarks → CR knees."
- "**Gap balancing** → tibia first, femoral rotation from the balanced flexion gap → PCL-resected knees."
- "**Hybrid** → distal femur, tibia, balance extension, then finish femur → what most do."

### Sequence
- Exposure → cuts → balancing → implantation → closure · cuts make gaps, balancing equalises them
- Implanting before balanced trials → locks the error in

### Measured resection
- Bone removed = **component thickness** (10 mm → 10 mm) · soft tissue ignored at this stage
- Rotation from **landmarks** · designed for **CR** (cruciate-retaining, posterior cruciate ligament intact) knees

#### Pros & cons
- Pros → joint line kept, **patellar tracking**, alignment, reproducible
[[FIG: Fig 10.17 · 10.4
- Cons → landmarks hard to palpate · **PCA** (posterior condylar axis) wrong in hypoplasia or valgus erosion
- Releases after all cuts → flexion imbalance → **lift-off** at 0–90° → eccentric polyethylene wear · lecturer dislikes it

### Gap balancing
- **Tibia first** → femoral rotation from a symmetric flexion gap: extension 15 mm → flexion 15 mm
[[FIG: Fig 10.18 · 10.4
- Ignores TEA and Whiteside line · for **PCL-resected**, PS (posterior-stabilised) knees
- Pros → flexion gap always **rectangular** → no lift-off, no eccentric load, no loosening

| Gap balancing con | Why |
|---|---|
| **Joint line elevation** | big deformity → more resection → relative baja |
| **Mid-flexion instability** | tight posterior capsule · tested at 0° and 90°, 45° forgotten |
| Non-anatomic rotation | landmarks ignored |
| Lost **posterior condylar offset** | big distal cut → big posterior cut → less flexion, impingement |

### Hybrid & instruments
- Anatomic position + balanced gaps → most surgeons, all current **instrument systems**
[[FIG: Fig 10.19 · 10.4
- Order → **distal femur** → tibia → balance extension gap → finish femur (flexion gap) → trials
- Never finish the femur first → extension gap tested first · bone removed is irreversible
- Beginners → measured · experienced → gaps · balancing either way → 11 Balancing

#### Cutting methods
- Conventional · **navigation** · robotic · PSI (patient-specific instrumentation, 3D-printed block, not in Egypt)
- Navigation → live alignment feedback · wrong **registration** → everything wrong
[[FIG: Fig 10.20 · 10.4
- Every implant has its own technique → request it · demo + **Sawbones** case first

### Alignment philosophies
| Philosophy | Idea |
|---|---|
| **Mechanical** (neutral) | tibia and femur cut at 90°, parallel → most common |
| **Anatomic** (Hungerford, 1980s) | tibia at native 87°, femur parallel → line inclined 2–3° |
| **Adjusted mechanical** | constitutional deformity kept, max 3° |
| **Kinematic** | native alignment kept → needs robot or navigation |
| **Restricted kinematic** | big deformity corrected only to a safe zone (40° → 7–10°) |

- Anatomic → some left in varus, inconsistent · 90° cut not physiological
[[FIG: Fig 10.21 · 10.4
- Kinematic claims → faster recovery, better satisfaction → **not proven**, not standard (Prof Sherif Khaled)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Measured = landmarks, CR · gaps = tibia first, PS · hybrid = distal femur → tibia → rest**
